summary: This experimental document defines the PIM Flooding Mechanism and Source Discovery for multicast. It lets sources be discovered by flooding information across the PIM domain, avoiding the need for a Rendezvous Point for that purpose. It is an alternative to relying only on shared trees from an RP.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking one office who is broadcasting, the news is shouted to everyone so all know who is on air.

questions: what is the pim flooding mechanism
how to discover multicast sources without a rendezvous point
how does pfm source discovery work

pim sm without a rendezvous point
subtitle: Flood the list of active multicast sources through a PIM network so routers can skip Rendezvous Points and shared trees.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM relies on a Rendezvous Point and shared trees to introduce new multicast sources, which adds configuration, operational work and a single point to reach.
tldr.mechanism: Routers flood PIM Flooding Mechanism (PFM) messages hop by hop. The first-hop router announces each active source and group in a Group Source Holdtime TLV, and receiving routers join the source tree directly.
tldr.outcome: Data flows only on shortest path trees and the network keeps working in partitions, but the first packets from a new source are dropped. The RFC is Experimental, with open questions about scale.

today: RFC 8364 is an Experimental RFC and has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Flood Source Information
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM, RFC 7761), a Rendezvous Point (RP) and shared trees carry multicast packets from new sources to Last-Hop Routers (LHRs). After the first packet arrives, the LHR learns the source and can join the Shortest Path Tree (SPT).

This RFC provides a way to run PIM-SM without PIM registers, RPs or shared trees. Source information is flooded through the multicast domain, so LHRs learn about new sources without receiving initial data packets. The authors argue this simplifies router operation and management, makes the protocol more robust, and sends data only on SPTs.

The RFC compares it to PIM Dense Mode with State-Refresh (RFC 3973), minus the initial flooding of data packets. It sits on top of the Source-Specific Multicast parts of PIM-SM (RFC 4607), as a source discovery mechanism for applications that do not do their own.
sections.eli5: Normally a middleman office introduces new broadcasters to viewers. Here the news about each new broadcaster is simply passed from neighbor to neighbor, so no middleman is needed.

sections.title: The PFM Message
sections.content:
The PIM Flooding Mechanism (PFM) generalizes the Bootstrap Router (BSR) flooding of RFC 5059. BSR can only distribute Group-to-RP mappings. PFM can carry any information, packed as TLVs, and any router can originate it, so there is no election as in BSR. Forwarding rules are identical to BSR, except that the message says whether routers must forward TLV types they do not support.

A PFM message is PIM message type 12. After the common PIM header it has a No-Forward bit, an Originator Address, and one or more TLVs. Each TLV has a Transitive bit, a 15-bit type (0 to 32767), a length and a value. A router that does not support a TLV type forwards it if and only if the Transitive bit is set.

Messages travel hop by hop and are link-local. The originator address never changes while the IP source address is that of the last forwarder. The originator MUST be routable in the domain, because forwarding uses RPF checks on it.
sections.eli5: Each message is a sealed envelope with a sender stamp and a list of notes. A router that does not understand a note passes it on anyway if the note is marked pass-it-on.

sections.title: Sending, Checking and Forwarding
sections.content:
A router MUST NOT originate more than Max_PFM_Message_Rate messages per minute (default 6) and MUST leave at least Min_PFM_Message_Gap milliseconds between them (default 1000). Both MUST be configurable. Combining TLVs in one message is RECOMMENDED, but messages should be small enough to avoid IP fragmentation. The originator address MUST NOT be link-local when not configured, and a virtual interface address is RECOMMENDED so it stays routable when links fail.

On receipt, a router drops the message unless it came from a directly connected PIM neighbor, was sent to ALL-PIM-ROUTERS, and did not arrive on an incoming administrative boundary. If the No-Forward bit is clear, it must come from the RPF neighbor of the originator address. The No-Forward bit is used only to help a new or restarted neighbor catch up, within 60 seconds of a PIM Hello, and such messages are not forwarded.

Valid messages are processed per TLV and then forwarded out of all interfaces with PIM neighbors, including the arrival interface. Administrative boundaries, which a router MUST be able to configure, can block all PFM messages or only certain TLVs on an interface.
sections.eli5: Routers only listen to notes from their neighbors, only in the right direction, and only a few notes per minute, so the notes cannot flood everything.

sections.title: Announcing and Joining Sources
sections.content:
The Group Source Holdtime (GSH) TLV is type 1 with the Transitive bit set. It carries a group address, a source count, a holdtime in seconds and a list of source addresses. The First-Hop Router (FHR) uses the usual PIM-SM rules to notice a new source, but instead of registering, it puts the source and group into a GSH TLV. Only the mapping is sent, not the packet itself.

GSH TLVs are re-announced every Group_Source_Holdtime_Period seconds (default 60) while the source is active. The holdtime is either zero or Group_Source_Holdtime_Holdtime (default 210, RECOMMENDED at 3.5 times the period). A holdtime of zero means the source is no longer active.

A router that receives a GSH TLV stores each mapping with an Expiry Timer. For each group with directly connected receivers it SHOULD send PIM (S,G) joins for the advertised sources. Source information MUST NOT be removed just because a source is missing from a later message, since many sources may be split across messages. A new source should trigger a message as soon as possible, subject to the rate limits.
sections.eli5: The router next to a broadcaster keeps shouting the broadcaster's name every minute. Routers with viewers hear it and tune in. If the shouting stops for a while, they forget the broadcaster.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Field Experience
sections.content:
The main cost is in Section 4.4: packets the FHR receives are dropped until the LHR has learned about the source and the SPT is built. That makes the approach a poor fit for bursty sources, such as one sending a packet every 4 minutes or less often, or for applications that depend on the first packets. It suits steady flows such as video distribution. For applications needing the initial packets, the RFC recommends BIDIR-PIM (RFC 5015) or SSM.

A benefit is resilience to network partitioning. Each partition keeps working independently and shares source mappings again after the network heals, whereas PIM-SM could need a candidate RP in every partition.

The RFC reports a prototype tested on a network with low-bandwidth radio links and frequent topology changes. Existing RP election was found too slow, and PIM-DM let new sources starve links. Applications including SIP with multicast subscriber discovery, multicast voice conferencing, position tracking and NTP were tested successfully, with limited field testing overall. The RFC is Experimental because open concerns remain about scale: processing per router, propagation delay, and how much source state can be distributed.
sections.eli5: The catch is that the first few seconds of a new show are missed while everyone tunes in. It works well for a show that never stops, and badly for one that only speaks now and then.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
PFM messages MUST only be accepted from a PIM neighbor, but any router can become a neighbor by sending a Hello. Operators can limit where PIM is enabled or configure administrative boundaries. A flood of forged PFM messages could stress every router. Forged GSH TLVs could announce a huge number of sources, so every router stores the state, and routers with interested receivers would build SPTs for sources that are not active.

Link-local PFM messages can be authenticated with IPsec per RFC 7761 and RFC 5796, which proves a trusted neighbor sent it. It does not prove the originator's information is correct, since that needs trusting every router along the path.

IANA registered PIM message type 12 and created the PFM TLV registry with the IETF Review policy. Type 0 is reserved, type 1 is the Source Group Holdtime, and 2 to 32767 are unassigned.
sections.eli5: A liar could shout fake broadcaster names and make everyone waste effort. Checking that notes come from trusted neighbors helps, but it cannot prove the first sender told the truth.
